sections.heading: Find the Problem, Then Say It Straight
body: A house that won't cool or heat is usually one failed part, not a dead system. A bad capacitor, a worn ignitor, a wiring fault, a leak in the refrigerant line.
But it can look the same as a system that's truly finished, and that's where people get talked into spending more than they had to.
A guess costs you twice: once for the part that didn't fix it, and again for the one that would have.
So we diagnose first. We tell you what failed, what it takes to fix, and whether the repair is worth making. If the answer is a repair, you get a repair.

sections.heading: AC Repair
body: Warm air from the vents, a unit that runs all day and never catches up, ice on the lines, water where it shouldn't be. Each of those points to something specific, and most of them get worse the longer the system keeps running.

We troubleshoot and diagnose your system, and we find refrigerant leaks. Low refrigerant means a leak somewhere, and topping it off without finding the leak only buys you a few weeks. We're EPA registered and certified to handle refrigerant.
We service all brands, so you don't have to be buying from us to call us.

sections.heading: Furnace Repair
body: A furnace that blows cold air, clicks and never lights, shuts off after a few minutes, or fills the house with a burning smell is telling you where to look. Ignitors wear out, flame sensors get dirty, wiring fails and filters choke off airflow.

We troubleshoot and diagnose, and we check for carbon monoxide, because a furnace that burns gas poorly can put it into the house without a smell or a warning. We repair furnaces, unit heaters and electric air handlers.

sections.heading: Air Quality and Carbon Monoxide Detection
body: Air in a closed house carries dust, pet dander and whatever your filter misses, and your system moves it through every room several times an hour.
We install filters in a range of sizes, and whole-system filtration that goes on any existing system and removes up to 90% of air contaminants.
Winter heat dries the air out, which is where the static shocks, cracked lips and gaps in the wood floors come from. A humidifier on the furnace puts that moisture back.
We also do carbon monoxide detection. If you burn gas for heat, it's worth having checked.

sections.heading: What "My AC Is Broken" Usually Means
body: An air conditioner has a few jobs: move refrigerant, push air across a cold coil, and push that air through your ducts. When the house stays warm, one of those jobs has stopped.

The usual signs are warm air from the vents, a system that runs and runs without catching up, ice on the lines or the indoor coil, a unit outside that hums but won't start, or water pooling near the indoor unit.
Each one points somewhere different. That's why a good repair starts with finding out which job failed, and why we show you which one it was before we fix it.

sections.heading: Why It Runs All Day and Never Catches Up
body: A system that runs constantly and leaves the house at 82 is working too hard for what it's getting. The common causes are low refrigerant, a coil caked with dirt, a clogged filter or leaky ducts.
Running it harder won't help. It wears the compressor, which is the most expensive part in the unit.
If the outdoor unit is blocked by grass clippings or a fence of weeds, clear them, but don't hose the coil while the system is running. Then call us.

sections.heading: Low Refrigerant Means a Leak
body: Refrigerant isn't used up like gas in a car. If your system is low, it leaked.
Adding more without finding the leak brings the same problem back. We do Freon leak detection so the repair fixes the leak, not just the symptom.
Refrigerant can only be handled by certified technicians, and we're EPA registered and certified.

We troubleshoot and diagnose before we recommend anything. That's how you find out whether you need a small part, something bigger, or nothing at all.

sections.heading: Ice on the Lines
body: Ice on the copper lines or the indoor coil means the coil is too cold to move heat. Poor airflow or low refrigerant is the usual reason.

Turn the system off and let it thaw, running just the fan if you can. If you keep running a frozen system, it can flood the drain pan and damage the compressor. We find out why it froze so it doesn't happen again next week.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace?
body: Most AC problems are repairs. A capacitor, a contactor or a fan motor is a small part, and a system that's still in decent shape is usually worth fixing.
A failed compressor on an older unit is where the math turns.

Replacement starts to make sense when the unit is old, repairs keep stacking up, or the repair would cost close to a new system. We'll tell you which situation you're in, and if it's a replacement, we install new air conditioners with equipment to fit your budget.

sections.heading: What Your Furnace Is Telling You
body: A furnace runs a sequence: the thermostat calls for heat, the ignitor lights the burners, the flame sensor confirms the flame, and the blower moves warm air through the house. If any step fails, the sequence stops.
That's why symptoms are so specific.

A furnace that clicks and never lights often has a worn ignitor. One that lights and shuts off a few minutes later may have a dirty flame sensor or poor airflow. A blower that won't start can be wiring or a failed part.
Telling these apart is the job. It's the difference between a quick repair and a guess, and we'll walk you through what we found.

sections.heading: Why a Furnace Blows Cold Air
body: Cold air from the vents doesn't always mean the furnace is dead. The blower runs on its own, so it can keep pushing air after the burners have shut off.

The cause is usually upstream: a flame that won't stay lit, a safety switch that tripped on overheating, or a filter so clogged the furnace can't breathe. Each has a different fix, and some of them are cheap.

sections.heading: Carbon Monoxide
body: A furnace that's burning gas poorly can put carbon monoxide into the house. You can't see or smell it.
We do carbon monoxide detection as part of our heating work. If you have a gas furnace and no working detector, ask us about it.
If you smell gas, don't stop to check the furnace. Leave the house and call the gas company from outside.
